lines: A root-cause question asks what the oven's temperature was at the exact moment a part went out of limits.
Matched on equal timestamps, the two sensors almost never land on the same instant, so the query comes back nearly empty.
Matched with no limit on how far back to look, it returns an answer every time, including one pulled from nearly an hour before.
For every reading on the fast, dense sensor, take the most recent reading from the slower, sparser one that happened at or before it.
That's the same backward-matching join already used earlier in this course for ordinary business facts.
Here it's simply matching two sensors against each other instead of a fact against a reference table.
Worth reasoning through before the next reveal answers it.
The two sensors' clocks are already known to disagree by some fixed, measured amount.
Setting the matching window tighter than that disagreement, does the join actually become more accurate?
answer: It doesn't, and that's the trap.
Below that clock disagreement, every match being excluded was already correct, so tightening further only throws good matches away.

lines: Put it to the test directly.
A matching window narrower than the clocks' own known disagreement excludes at least as many matches as one set right at that disagreement.
Nothing is gained by going tighter, and genuinely correct matches are lost.
Running the identical join through two completely different engines, they agree on every single row.
As the matching window shrinks past how often the slower sensor actually reports, the share of unmatched rows climbs away from zero.
Right at that reporting rate, and wider, every row still finds a match.
On a signal whose true path between samples is already known, a plain backward match just holds the last reading flat until a newer one arrives.
Filling in the point between the sample before and the sample after recovers something much closer to the signal's real path.
That better value only exists by looking at a sample that, in a live system, hasn't happened yet.
Without first grouping the match by which piece of equipment each reading came from, a reading from one machine can get paired with the nearest reading from a completely different one.
No error gets raised anywhere in that process.
The row that comes back simply looks plausible and is quietly wrong.
A backward match takes whatever was most recently true at or before a given moment.
A matching window tighter than a known clock disagreement helps nothing at all.
A more accurate value bought by looking ahead carries the same cost as a feature that leaks the future.
And grouping by equipment first isn't an optional tuning step, it's what keeps the match honest.
One more case worth reasoning through before moving on.
A separate pipeline's matching join has no limit on staleness and no grouping by equipment at all, and it has never once come back empty.
Does never once coming back empty count as a sign that this join is working well?
answer: It doesn't. That's close to the opposite of a good sign.

With no staleness limit, nothing is ever too old to count, and with no grouping, nothing is ever rejected for coming from the wrong machine — never coming back empty is exactly what that combination guarantees.
